newsitem.title: USA: Continental Air reaches new status with alliance.
newsitem.headline: Continental Air reaches new status with alliance.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc's proposed code-sharing alliance with Virgin Atlantic Airways gives the Houston-based carrier highly coveted access to London's Heathrow Airport and boosts the airline to first class status, analysts said.
"Clearly, getting into the Heathrow market is a major upgrade of Continental's international product," said Candace Browning, an airline analyst with Merrill Lynch.
Analysts said the proposed link with Virgin is the clearest signal Continental has put to rest its beleagured reputation and has built its Newark hub into an international power.

"It is validation that Continental has joined the ranks of airlines that Virgin would be willing to attach its name to. It says Virgin is willing to bet its quality reputation on Continental," said Tom Schreier, an analyst with CS First Boston.
"It means that Continental become a real option for business travelers."
Continental and Virgin said their new code-sharing partnership will replace Virgin's exisiting alliance with Delta Air Lines Inc, which will end later this year.

Delta's relationship with Virgin "was no longer commerically beneficial," said Delta spokesman Bill Berry. Delta declined to comment on how much it gained from its alliance with Virgin, which began in 1995.

Delta said it recently attempted to renegotiate its pact with Virgin because the competitive environment has changed over the past two years. Delta said it decided to end the Virgin alliance when new terms could not be reached.

Analysts said Delta was not generating enough revenue from the deal to justify the investment. Delta's strong presence at New York's Kennedy Airport also made it a less attractive companion for Virgin, which flies to Newark, analysts said.
Delta will use its other international alliances with carriers such as Air France to offset any business lost from the Virgin pact, analysts said.
Continental declined to comment on how much it expects to gain from its new relationship with Virgin.
The company has previously said its pacts with Air France, Alitalia and Aeroflot generate about $70 million in annual revenues.
Although Continental will gain some access to Heathrow, the carrier will not quiet its opposition to the proposed mega-alliance between British Airways Plc and AMR Corp's American Airlines.

"Although this arrangement will give Continental limited access to Heathrow, it's nowhere near what we need to counter the juggernaut being proposed by British Airways and American Airlines," said Gordon M. Bethune, Continental's chairman and chief executive officer.
"If that anti-competitive transaction is approved, Continental alone will need at least 140 Heathrow slots even to begin to compete effectively," Bethune said.
Both Continental and Virgin have been outspoken opponents, saying the BA-American pact would create a monopoly that would restrict competition and hurt consumers.
Currently, only British Airways, United, American Airlines, Virgin Atlantic can operate U.S. services out of Heathrow.
